newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-PLAYERS FIND U.S. OPEN 18TH HOLE SHORT AND SWEET.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-PLAYERS FIND U.S. OPEN 18TH HOLE SHORT AND SWEET.

text.p: The finish to this year's U.S. Open, which starts on Thursday at Congressional Country Club, figures to be short and sweet since the national championship ends on par-3 for the first time in 88 years.
"It's a great hole," said three-time Masters and British Open champion Nick Faldo.
"Overall, I think it's a perfect hole," said 1997 Masters hero Tiger Woods.
Davis Love, runner-up at last year's Open, said: "I think it's a great hole and a neat finish."
Twice British Open winner Greg Norman, who questioned finishing on a par-3 before he came to Congressional this week and played it, said: "I think this hole fits the situation beautifully."

The Open last finished on a par-3 in 1909 at Englewood Golf Club. Three previous Opens finished on par-3s -- in 1896 at Shinnecock Hills, in 1898 at Myopia Hunt Club and in 1902 at Garden City Golf Club.
At the 18th at Englewood, 1909 winner George Sargent drove within six feet of the hole and made the putt to become the only Open champion ever to make a two on the final hole.
A par-3, of course, could yield an even lower number on the climactic hole. Former British Open champion Mark Calcavecchia aced the 18th in practice on Tuesday.
One's appreciation of the 190-yard 18th, guarded by water on three sides, could well depend on one's position on the leaderboard.
Some players say it would be a relief to arrive protecting a lead since a routine par would be available without having to drive the ball and risk landing in rough.

"I think that the guys are finding that it's a pretty easy hole compared to some of the other ones because you get to tee the ball up and hit a 5-iron from a perfect lie to a fairly big green," said Love.
"I'd much rather play that hole having to make par than 16 or 17 because those holes are extremely difficult."
Former Masters champion Ian Woosnam, the current money leader on the European tour, followed Love to the podium in the interview room.
"I like the way Davis said it was an easy hole. When you're standing there, hitting the green is a different ball game altogether."
Woods was thinking along the same lines as Love.

"I think if you're behind, it's a tough, tough hole to make shots up on," said Woods, knowing that tight pin placements would heighten the dangers of splashing in the water with an aggressive swing for the stick.

"If you have a lead, it's in your favour because it's not that hard to put an iron on the green. If 17 was the finishing hole (which it was at the 1964 Open here) I think that would be more difficult. Then you bring a double (bogey) in the equation with a bad drive or something like that."
Reigning British Open champion Tom Lehman said that coupled with the long, 480-yard, water-guarded 17th, the Open ending could sizzle.
"It's a great finish. The 17th hole is one of the great par-4s in golf and then 18 is a good par-3. You can see everything when you're coming down the fairway," said Lehman.

"If you are the kind of guy that likes to watch what's going on around him and you're in the hunt and you see a guy make a long one for a birdie on 18 while you're walking down the fairway on 17, that's pretty good drama."
Faldo said the 18th would test players' strategic thinking.

"There are an awful lot of permutations depending on your position, since you're on the 72nd hole. You know, if you're leading, or by how many, or if you're trailing or whatever you need. It's going to create a big decision shot.
"I played a 4-iron yesterday so it's not as if it's a little, easy 9-iron across the water. Just hitting it in the middle of the green is a hell of a shot."
